description: We are a passionate team of builders, researchers, and problem solvers dedicated to creating reliable, real world space and aviation solutions. Our collective background blends machine learning, stochastic modeling, and hands on hardware prototyping.
summary:
Safety First: Beyond the Horizon is an offline research workspace that turns scattered NASA fire-safety research into a clear starting point for Moon and Mars missions. We developed a single web tool that collects 20 NASA combustion investigations, ranks them for a chosen mission scenario such as a lunar habitat, compares studies side by side, and shows exactly where evidence is missing.

It answers the Flame in Freefall challenge directly. Fire behaves differently in microgravity and partial gravity, yet there is very little verified data for the Moon (0.167 g) and Mars (0.38 g). Our tool puts NASA open data at its core, shows what is known, and marks what is not, so researchers know which experiments to use and where new tests are needed.

It matters because crews will live in oxygen-enriched, low-pressure habitats where Earth-based fire assumptions may not hold. Better evidence about fire supports safer missions, and NASA fire research has already led to benefits on Earth, such as better firefighter gear and lighter air tanks.
details:
How it works. Users select a mission profile, for example a lunar habitat at 34% oxygen. The workspace ranks the 20 NASA investigations by relevance to that profile, shows each study’s evidence coverage, and lets users compare up to four studies side by side. A gravity lab plots two clearly labelled what-if curves between 0 g and 1 g. An offline assistant answers questions using only the loaded data.

NASA data used.

  • 20 NASA combustion investigations (ACME, BASS, Saffire, FLEX, SAME and more) covering gas, solid, liquid, aerosol and dust fuels, across six hardware ecosystems and three safety domains: prevention, detection and suppression.
  • 6 run conditions from NASA technical reports (NTRS), labelled as literature values, not PSI telemetry.
  • Each study links to its NASA sources. The PSI archive could not be retrieved, so we claim no PSI accession IDs. Syncing run-level PSI data is our next step.

What makes it creative. Existing resources show one study at a time. Our tool ranks all studies for your mission and highlights the gaps, so it shows where nobody has looked yet.

Factors we considered.

  • Missing data stays missing and is never counted as zero.
  • Burner-stream oxygen (up to 85% in one experiment) is kept out of cabin-air matching.
  • Scores measure relevance, not safety.
  • The gravity lab is a what-if, not a prediction.
  • It runs in any browser with no install, account or server. New missions or datasets are added as data rows.

Tools. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one file, NASA pages and technical reports as sources, and Claude for development support.
